note: Concept index. These are the atlas’s analytical terms, not native categories. Each one is defined here so that its use in the plates is consistent.

concepts.name: Threshold
concepts.gloss: The border between the living and the dead, maintained by prohibitions rather than by a wall.
concepts.description: Used for the set of small adjustments made around a death: the opened window, the covered mirror, the stopped clock, the body carried out. The term is analytical; the sources describe the practices, not the concept.

concepts.name: Soul
concepts.gloss: The part of the person that survives death; described in both theological and folk registers.
concepts.description: Orthodox doctrine and folk belief use the same word (*dusha*) for different constructions: a created immortal substance judged by God, and a breath-like presence that lingers near the body and must be fed and escorted. The atlas keeps the registers apart.

concepts.name: Return
concepts.gloss: The dead coming back, or being treated as if they might.
concepts.description: The returning dead are a way of talking about unfinished obligation. The atlas distinguishes the ethnographic reports (documented) from the category built on them (interpretation).

concepts.name: Purification
concepts.gloss: The washing of the body and the separation of the living from the dead.
concepts.description: Washing is both practical and symbolic. The atlas treats it as a technique for handling the dead at arm’s length, and avoids claims about its pre-Christian origin.

concepts.name: Mourning
concepts.gloss: The social and emotional work of loss, performed in public or withheld.
concepts.description: In the Russian twentieth century mourning was repeatedly reorganised: by the Church, by the Soviet state and by the family. The atlas follows the distinction between public commemoration and private grief.

concepts.name: Remembrance
concepts.gloss: The scheduled repetition of prayer, food and naming.
concepts.description: Remembrance in this atlas is a calendar and a set of objects: days three, nine and forty, the annual commemoration, the meal, the name spoken aloud. It is the most documented form of relation with the dead.

concepts.name: Memory
concepts.gloss: The use of the dead by the living — personal, familial, national.
concepts.description: Memory is treated here as a practice with owners and budgets. The state’s memory is built at memorial complexes; the family’s memory at the table and at the grave.

concepts.name: Abandonment
concepts.gloss: The state of a grave, a cemetery or a name that no one maintains.
concepts.description: Abandonment is not the absence of memory but its entropy. The atlas documents it as a condition of the material record, and marks its own inability to survey it.

concepts.name: Afterlife
concepts.gloss: The imagined geography of the dead.
concepts.description: The atlas distinguishes the doctrinal claim (judgement, resurrection, communion with God) from the iconographic and folk geography (scales, rivers of fire, roads, places of waiting).
